Package org.apache.juneau.examples.mcp.secured

Class OfflineAuthorizationServer

java.lang.Object
org.apache.juneau.examples.mcp.secured.OfflineAuthorizationServer
All Implemented Interfaces:
AutoCloseable
public final class OfflineAuthorizationServer extends Object implements AutoCloseable
A minimal, self-contained, in-process stand-in for a real OAuth 2.1 authorization server (AS), so the secured MCP example (and its end-to-end test) run entirely offline — no external IdP, no network access, no pre-shared secrets checked into source control.

DEMO ONLY — NOT SUITABLE FOR PRODUCTION USE.

This is deliberately NOT a general-purpose or spec-complete authorization server. It exists purely to make SecuredExampleMcpServer's JwtTokenValidator-backed resource-server gate and SecuredExampleClient's McpTokenProvider-backed client-credentials flow both have something real to talk to. Concretely, on start() it:

  1. Generates a fresh RSA-2048 signing key (a new key every run — nothing is persisted, so restarting the example invalidates any previously-issued token, which is exactly the offline-demo property we want).
  2. Publishes only the public half of that key as a JWKSource, which SecuredExampleMcpServer feeds directly to JwtTokenValidator.jwkSource(...) — no JWKS HTTP endpoint is needed because the server and "AS" share this JVM.
  3. Starts a tiny HttpServer exposing two routes:
    • POST /token — the RFC 6749 §4.4 client-credentials grant against one fixed, randomly-generated demo client id/secret pair (see clientId() / clientSecret()). This is a REAL HTTP round trip: the client-side OAuthClientCredentialsFlow used by McpTokenProvider talks to it exactly as it would talk to a production IdP's token endpoint, just on localhost.
    • GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server — a minimal RFC 8414 Authorization Server Metadata document (issuer + token_endpoint only), so a real client can perform genuine discovery against issuerUri() instead of being handed the token endpoint out of band. See SecuredExampleClient for the client half of that handshake.

What this class intentionally does NOT implement (called out here and in the README so nobody mistakes this demo for a template for a real deployment):

  • No real scope-authorization decision — handleToken(com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpExchange) only checks the requested scope against a fixed allowlist (mcp.read/mcp.write); it never asks a resource owner or policy engine whether the client is ALLOWED that scope, which is what a real AS's consent/policy step does.
  • No refresh tokens, no consent screen, no user authentication of any kind — only the machine-to-machine client-credentials grant, which is all an MCP server-to-server OAuth demo needs.
  • No persistence, replay protection beyond the JWT exp/nbf window, or key rotation. The RFC 8414 document above is likewise minimal: no jwks_uri, no scopes_supported, no dynamic client registration — this AS's public key is handed directly to the validator in-process (see jwkSource()) rather than published for a real JWKS fetch.

TLS caveat: this class and SecuredExampleServer talk plain http only because both ends are loopback-only (127.0.0.1/localhost). OAuth 2.1 / RFC 9728 require https for any non-loopback resource identifier or token endpoint; a bearer token sent over plaintext to a non-loopback host is exposed to anyone on the network path.

A real deployment would point JwtTokenValidator at an actual IdP's JWKS URL and issuer, and would never generate or hand out client secrets like start() does here.
